prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping brought frequency standards to the 10^-18 level and opened new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs observation, but I move the optical lattice clock to the head of my list after reading the other seven ballots. It is the one shortlisted candidate that every colleague ranked, five of us in the top three and three first places, and the reasons given are scientific, not merely social. The magic-wavelength idea removes Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts at the same time, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once. That gave a 10^-18 instrument that has been rebuilt and cross-checked in many national laboratories. It already measures gravitational redshift across millimetres, and it constrains drifts of constants and some dark-matter couplings. That ties it to the questions in gravity and cosmology that I care about most, and it shows the 'clues from nature' approach I favour. Attribution is also the cleanest on the table: Katori proposed the lattice and made the first demonstrations, and Ye's group took it to record accuracy and combined it with comb technology. Two names, a clear citation, mature field, and a redefinition of the second that gives it timeliness.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is an invention of an instrument and a precision frontier, not yet a discovery about nature, and my own stated standard is that discoveries come first and people second. No deviation from general relativity or the Standard Model has been found with lattice clocks, so the fundamental-physics payoff is so far a promise. The committee has also rewarded the neighbouring ground twice, combs in 2005 (Hall and Hansch) and ion-based control of single quantum systems in 2012 (Wineland), and a sceptic can call lattice clocks the natural successor and so a smaller step. Ion clocks, notably Al+ clocks, were also developed in parallel and may be argued as co-equal. Finally, I am giving up the Higgs observation, which is the clearest 'nature answered the question' discovery in the field but which I could not attach to a defensible three-person credit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because progress is limited by what we can measure, with 10^-18 uncertainties feeding geodesy, constants tests and the redefinition of the second, and he sees the work as distinct from the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I agree on the distinction from the comb prize: a comb is a ruler, whereas the lattice clock is a new way of holding the reference atoms. I would, though, ask for more than the redefinition of the second as justification. A redefinition is a metrological milestone, not a physical discovery. The case becomes stronger for me if the expert reports show that lattice-clock comparisons have already produced a competitive bound on constants or on ultralight dark matter, not just the promise of one. I accept your credit allocation but want that evidence before the final ballot.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength idea is a clean piece of atomic physics where theory and experiment agree, and warns that overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes may weigh against it and that a third contributor is not settled.
responses.response: Your point on overlap is the right worry, and I take it more seriously than my opening ranking at fifth place suggests. Where I differ is on a third name. The supplied credit is compact, and I would not add one just to look generous: Lemonde, Derevianko and others contributed, but the decisive concept and the decisive performance record sit with Katori and Ye. If you think a third contributor has a real claim to the concept, I would like to hear who, and on what primary-literature evidence, rather than on the grounds that the field is large.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a simple mechanism with broad consequences, with Kane and Mele supplying the decisive theory and Molenkamp the HgTe observation, and he accepts the overlap with the 2016 prize as a risk.
responses.response: I share your admiration for the Z2 idea and had it fourth. My difficulty is the one Eriksson, Johansson and Lindroth also raised and you acknowledge: the HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not on the supplied credit, and the 3D materials belong to Fu, Kane, Moore and Hasan. A prize that rewards the first experiment while leaving out the proposal that told experimenters what to build looks unfair, and it comes only a decade after the 2016 topology prize. I regard that as a more severe allocation problem than the one for lattice clocks, so I would not put it at the head of the list, although I do not think it is a weak discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as a prediction of flat bands followed by a decisive experiment, and he would prefer two laureates, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, since Bistritzer is a less natural third.
responses.response: I understand the appeal of theory meeting measurement, and the phenomenon has been reproduced widely. But the field is under ten years old, and Mehlig, Johansson and Lindroth each say the pairing mechanism is unresolved. I am wary of elegant theory that has not been settled by nature, and I would rather wait until the origin of the superconductivity is understood than honour the platform now. I also share your reservation that the experimental credit leaves out the first author and fabrication pioneers, which makes the three-name credit less clean than it looks. If you can show that the central claim is robust against twist-angle disorder, I would reconsider, but today I rank it below the clocks.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first as a new observational window built on a detector concept, and accepts that the two-name credit of Halzen and Spiering is workable although AMANDA and Baikal pioneers complicate it.
responses.response: IceCube is the candidate closest to my own preference for discoveries made by nature, and I had it third. I keep it as an alternative. My doubt is attribution, which you also flag: Halzen conceived and drove the project, but Spiering's role is more as a long-time leader of the programme than as the person who made the central discovery, and the 2013 observation was made by a collaboration of hundreds. I would want the expert reports to say who is decisive for the diffuse-flux detection, and whether the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 results are firm enough that we are not rewarding a field that is still defining itself. If those reports are strong, I would happily support a configuration led by neutrino astronomy.

uncertainties: Whether lattice-clock comparisons have produced a competitive bound on constants, dark matter or gravity, or whether the physics payoff is still prospective.
How strongly the 2005 and 2012 prizes should count against a third prize in precision atomic metrology and whether Al+ ion-clock work has a co-equal claim.
Whether an Higgs-observation prize, which only I ranked, can be given a defensible credit among thousands of ATLAS and CMS members, and whether the 2013 theory prize makes it redundant.
Whether the IceCube source-identification evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is judged as firm as the diffuse-flux detection, and who is decisive for it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: I have no known personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted candidates. My mentors and frequent co-authors (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet) are not on the shortlist. I note only that the black-hole shadow candidate lies close to my own research interests, and that is not a reason for recusal.
